title: Ancient constellations over ALMA
caption: The Pleiades and Orion over ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: ALMA's antennas, part of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, stand under a sky crowded with stars in this photograph by ESO Photo Ambassador Babak Tafreshi. In the upper left corner glows a tight bunch of young stars, the Pleiades cluster, surprisingly bright. The constellation of Orion, the Hunter, hangs over the nearest antenna, and the three blue stars just left of the red light form his belt.
The clear skies over the Chajnantor Plateau show thousands of stars to the naked eye. That dry, transparent air is one of the reasons ALMA was built here.

The scene also carries an old story. The Pleiades were known to most ancient civilisations, and in classical mythology Orion was a hunter who pursued the Pleiades, the daughters of Atlas. Through the thin air over the Atacama, it almost looks as if the chase is really taking place.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph at the ALMA site, in visible light. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: The caption notes that thousands of stars are visible to the naked eye here, but a camera exposure gathers more light still, so star colours and faint stars show more clearly.

explore: ESO calls ALMA the biggest astronomical project in the world. Europe, North America and East Asia run it jointly, in cooperation with the Republic of Chile, with each region's share led by ESO, the National Radio Astronomy Observatory and the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan.
alt: ALMA antennas under a starry sky, with a bright star cluster in the upper left and a row of three blue stars above the nearest antenna.
